book: How Search Decides What You See
author: Aaron Tay

episodes.title: How words become a search vector
episodes.subtitle: Inside the retrieval encoder

scenes.title: A language model is only the beginning
scenes.claim: Text → model tokens → contextual vectors → pooling
scenes.narration: Imagine a tiny factory that turns a question into coordinates. A language model supplies some machinery, but search needs a representation it can store and compare. Chapter six opens that factory, from input tokens to one retrieval vector.

scenes.title: Two kinds of token, two different jobs
scenes.claim: An indexed term has postings. A model token enters an encoder.
scenes.narration: First, a naming trap. Lexical analysis makes index terms, which point to posting lists. A model tokeniser makes input units for an encoder. These units interact with their neighbours. Calling both tokens does not make them interchangeable.

scenes.title: A string can be split without being understood
scenes.claim: Illustrative split; actual pieces depend on the tokeniser
scenes.narration: An unfamiliar word such as delulu may be split into reusable pieces. Some tokenisers work with characters or bytes instead. That improves input coverage. It does not prove that the model understands the slang, the question, or the searcher's need.

scenes.title: Pieces become IDs, then initial vectors
scenes.claim: Toy IDs and dimensions: these are inputs, not search coordinates
scenes.narration: Each input piece maps to an identifier in the model's fixed vocabulary or byte inventory. A lookup supplies an initial vector for that identifier. Our little coloured grids are a toy illustration. These are still token representations, before the model reads the context.

scenes.title: The neighbours change the representation
scenes.claim: Self-attention produces contextual token representations
scenes.narration: Now the encoder reads the tokens together. Self-attention lets their representations use information from surrounding tokens. A job in an interview question gains context that the same input word in an agricultural history would not have. The model still produces per-token representations.

scenes.title: Many token vectors become one
scenes.claim: Mean pooling is one option; a sequence-opening representation is another
scenes.narration: Pooling combines that working material into one representation for the whole query or passage. One common approach averages the contextual token vectors. Another uses the sequence-opening representation. The pooled coordinates are not a list of searchable words, and token-level detail becomes harder to inspect.

scenes.title: Encode the question and passage separately
scenes.claim: Bi-encoder: independent representations, then a similarity score
scenes.narration: In a bi-encoder, query and passage travel through separate encoding paths. Their parameters may be shared or distinct. The resulting vectors can be compared with a similarity function. Passage vectors can be prepared before a new query arrives, making this arrangement useful for search.

scenes.title: The factory needs a lesson in retrieval
scenes.claim: Pooling gives a vector. Retrieval training teaches useful comparisons.
scenes.narration: But producing a vector is not the same as producing a good search vector. Language pretraining alone does not ensure that an answer scores above a merely related passage. The next film teaches the factory what should rank together. Chapter seven then puts those vectors into a collection-scale index.

episodes.title: Teaching an encoder what to retrieve
episodes.subtitle: Positives, negatives, and the searcher's need

scenes.title: Nearby is not automatically useful
scenes.claim: Pretraining learns language patterns; retrieval training targets comparisons
scenes.narration: Two texts can sound similar without one answering a search for the other. Predicting masked or next tokens teaches language patterns. Retrieval needs a different lesson: which passage should score higher for this particular query? Pooling a language model alone does not settle that question.

scenes.title: What does the searcher actually need?
scenes.claim: Teaching case: help me judge whether my expectations are unrealistic
scenes.narration: Take the chapter's question: am I being delulu about getting this job? For this teaching case, we interpret the need as judging unrealistic expectations. That interpretation matters. The training labels follow a stated need, not a universal meaning hidden in the words.

scenes.title: Choose a labelled positive
scenes.claim: Relevant for the stipulated need, even without identical vocabulary
scenes.narration: The labelled positive explains how to recognise unrealistic expectations during a job search. It addresses the stipulated need, although it does not repeat the slang. Training encourages its vector to receive a higher similarity score with the query than competing passages.

scenes.title: An easy negative is a distant competitor
scenes.claim: Agricultural employment shares a broad employment theme
scenes.narration: An easy negative is a history of agricultural employment. It concerns work, but it does little to help this searcher judge their expectations. Easy negatives can supply useful contrast. They do not necessarily teach the finer distinctions inside a closely related topic.

scenes.title: The hard negative sounds almost right
scenes.claim: Same broad topic; a different question under this interpretation
scenes.narration: Now the tricky competitor: ten signs that you performed well in your job interview. It shares the topic and important vocabulary. Here it is a hard negative because our need concerns unrealistic expectations. For someone estimating their chances from an interview, it might instead be useful.

scenes.title: Teach the ordering, change the geometry
scenes.claim: Illustrative 2D geometry and cosine scores; no trained model is measured
scenes.narration: Training updates model parameters to favour the labelled positive over the alternatives. Triplet and contrastive objectives implement this idea in different ways. Our moving dots illustrate a desired ordering, not measured model behaviour. Which negatives you choose changes the distinctions the model is encouraged to learn.

scenes.title: The lesson matters as much as the machinery
scenes.claim: SBERT: efficient sentence comparison. DPR: question–passage retrieval.
scenes.narration: Sentence BERT adapted BERT for efficient comparison of independently encoded sentences. Dense Passage Retrieval trained question and passage encoders for retrieval. Both show the key transition: train the representations for the comparison you need. Simply choosing a familiar language-model family is not enough.

scenes.title: A high score is still a learned signal
scenes.claim: Training labels are task-dependent; similarity is not a relevance probability
scenes.narration: The trained space rewards relationships that its examples and objective taught it to preserve. A similarity score is not a probability of relevance. Positive and negative labels depend on the task. Next, we ask where those labels came from, and whose idea of usefulness they encode.

episodes.title: Whose relevance does the model learn?
episodes.subtitle: Training signals and library judgement

scenes.title: Every training signal tells a different story
scenes.claim: Human judgements · clicks · answer pairs · citations · generated queries
scenes.narration: Who decided which texts belong together? Retrieval training can use human judgements, clicked results, question and answer pairs, citations, generated queries, or other proxies. Those sources teach different versions of a useful result. The same architecture can become a different retriever.

scenes.title: A click can reward visibility
scenes.claim: Clicks can reflect popularity and ranking position
scenes.narration: A click is an observed action, not a direct measurement of relevance. People can click a result because it is prominent or popular. Training on those actions can reward those patterns too. The supervision carries both useful information and the limitations of its source.

scenes.title: Answer pairs teach answer-bearing matches
scenes.claim: The training relationship shapes what similarity rewards
scenes.narration: Question and answer pairs encourage the model to find passages that answer questions. Titles paired with abstracts may teach more about topical similarity. Both can be useful, but they reward different relationships. Neither guarantees that a retrieved paper satisfies an evidence review's eligibility criteria.

scenes.title: Citations teach scholarly relatedness
scenes.claim: SPECTER uses citation relationships for paper embeddings
scenes.narration: The chapter gives SPECTER as a scholarly example. Citation relationships help train document embeddings so that linked papers are drawn together. That is a useful model of scholarly relatedness. It is different from finding a direct answer to every query, or proving a paper's findings.

scenes.title: Same architecture, different education
scenes.claim: Collection, language, discipline, and task can differ from training
scenes.narration: A retriever trained on general web questions has learnt from that setting. A chemistry collection, another language, or systematic-review searching may require different distinctions. Architecture alone does not guarantee transfer. Evaluate the model on the collection, query population, and task you actually care about.

scenes.title: Small differences may carry the whole question
scenes.claim: Identifiers, contradictions, and specialised senses need to matter in training
scenes.narration: If training rarely rewards exact identifiers, a vector may blur them. If negatives rarely contain contradictions or specialised senses, those distinctions may be weak too. Our invented compound identifiers illustrate why two nearly identical strings can demand very different retrieval decisions.

scenes.title: Poor results need a diagnosis
scenes.claim: Check coverage, fields, query processing, and cut-offs; evaluate locally
scenes.narration: Poor chemistry results make training mismatch plausible, but do not establish the cause. First inspect collection coverage, searchable fields, query processing, and candidate cut-offs. Then compare performance across a local set of judged queries. Several parts of the pipeline can produce the same missing-paper symptom.

scenes.title: Three questions to take back to the library
scenes.claim: What is encoded? What taught similarity? Does it work for our task?
scenes.narration: Take three questions with you. What does each stored vector represent? Which positives, negatives, and training signals taught its similarities? Does it retrieve useful material for our own task? Model tokens enter an encoder; retrieval training shapes its comparisons; evidence from your collection tests whether that lesson was useful.
